In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the integration of endosymbiontic systems can be assessed, and what the consequences for our nomenclature are.
the question of whether a given endosymbiotic relationship is a “host/symbiosis” or an “eukaryotic/organelle” system.
the question of how organelles can be distinguished from symbionts.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“the host/symbionts are one species” and “the eukaryotic organelles are part of the host”.
“organelles” are endosymbiontic systems that cannot evolve independently of their hosts, whereas symbionts are endosymbiotic partners that can evolve independently of their host species.
the term organelle is a misnomer for all symbiotic organelles.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the endosymbiotic relationship between the dinoflagellate Karenia brevis and its symbiont, a member of the Alphaproteobacteria, is a sexual symbiont integrated system.
we are able to show that the endosymbiotic relationship between a cyanobacterial endosymbion and its amoebal host is not a stable one and is therefore not suitable for the definition of a species.
mitochondria and plastid are organelles, whereas the endosymbiotic bacteria that live in the mitochondria and plastida of some eukaryotes, are symbionts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distinction between “symbiont” vs. “organelle” should be based on whether or not the endosymbiosis prevents independent speciation.
the distinction between “organelle” and “symbiont” should be based on the integration of the partners in speciation and not on the integration of genes, metabolism or cellular processes.
the distinction between host and symbiont should not be based on a particular mechanism or structure of a given system.
